strengths: Novel and reasonably well-motivated hierarchical dual-encoder design that explicitly separates sleep micro-structure (short-term signal morphology) from macro-structure (full-night architecture), addressing a real gap in the sleep foundation model literature where prior work (e.g., SleepFM) focuses mainly on local/epoch-level representations.

The proposed Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) objective is a creative way to obtain a noise-free, scalable supervisory signal for macro-structure learning without relying on subjective/expert-scored labels, and is supported by clear exploratory evidence (Figures 4, 8, 9) showing that sleep stage trajectories differ systematically by age, sex, and BMI.

Large-scale, multi-dataset pretraining corpus (>20K recordings, 158K hours across 7 public cohorts) with careful preprocessing and channel harmonization, which is a nontrivial engineering contribution and improves the credibility of claimed generalizability.

Reasonably comprehensive downstream evaluation spanning sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease risk prediction (Cox PH), few-shot adaptation, and demographic probing, providing a multi-faceted view of representation quality rather than a single task.

Useful ablations (Table 11, Table 12) isolating the contribution of shared/private encoders, MAE, CL, large-scale pretraining, and DGCL, plus per-attribute analysis of which demographic signals (age/sex/BMI) help most.
Good documentation of architecture hyperparameters, training schedules, and dataset statistics in the appendix, which aids reproducibility even without released code.
weaknesses: Results are inconsistent across datasets and tasks in ways not fully resolved: on KISS, a generic time-series model (MOMENT) outperforms SleepMaMi on sleep staging, and on SHHS1 SDB segmentation UniTS achieves higher raw accuracy; the paper's explanation (Compumedics vs. Nox/Embla hardware distribution shift) is speculative and not empirically tested (e.g., no hardware-stratified ablation or domain adaptation experiment).

In the disease-prediction comparison (Table 3), SleepMaMi actually underperforms SleepFM-Disease on 3 of 6 outcomes (CVD death, CHD death, Stroke), yet the text frames this as 'comparable performance' without a more calibrated discussion of when/why the macro-structure signal helps or hurts.

The added value of DGCL specifically (as opposed to simply having more pretraining data and a Mamba-based macro-encoder) is only weakly isolated: Table 12 ablation trained solely on SHHS1 shows only ~1 percentage point gain from full DGCL (79.8% to 80.7%), which is a fairly marginal improvement and raises questions about how much of the large jump in Table 11 (79.8% to 81.9%) is attributable to DGCL versus other confounded factors such as increased Macro-Encoder capacity or additional Mamba layers.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported for any experiment; all comparisons rely on single-run point estimates, which is a significant limitation given several close margins (e.g., SDB accuracy differences on SHHS1 between SleepMaMi and SleepFM/UniTS).

Baseline comparisons may not be fully controlled: SleepFM-Disease is evaluated at a different sampling rate (256 Hz) than SleepMaMi's pipeline (100 Hz) per the baseline's specific requirements, which could confound the comparison, and no more recent or stronger sleep-specific SSL baselines beyond SleepFM/SleepFM-Disease are included.

Evaluation is dominated by linear probing; while this is reasonable for representation-quality assessment, the paper does not explore full fine-tuning (except briefly in the few-shot ISRUC setting, and even there only against SleepFM-Disease, omitting MOMENT/UniTS which were sometimes competitive earlier).

There is no explicit Limitations section, and ethical/fairness considerations around using demographic attributes (age, sex, BMI) as training signal for a clinical model are not discussed at all — e.g., potential propagation of demographic bias into downstream disease-risk predictions, or fairness concerns for underrepresented subgroups (the pretraining cohort skews heavily male in some datasets, e.g., MrOS is 100% male), which is a notable omission for a health-related foundation model.

No statement on code or model release, which combined with the complexity of the architecture (MoE, private-shared transformers, bi-directional Mamba, hierarchical patch merging) may hinder independent reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: Large and diverse pretraining corpus (20,964 PSG recordings, ~158K hours across 7 public datasets), which is a substantial engineering effort and a useful resource for the field.

The dual-encoder design that explicitly separates micro-structure (epoch-level biosignal morphology) from macro-structure (full-night architecture) is a reasonable and intuitively motivated architectural idea, and the Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) objective is a creative way to obtain label-free supervisory signal for macro-structure without relying on noisy manual sleep stage annotations.

Evaluation spans a reasonably diverse set of downstream tasks (sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction via Cox PH, few-shot adaptation, demographic regression), which is appropriate for a 'foundation model' claim.

Ablations (Table 11, 12) and embedding visualizations (UMAP, demographic stratified hypnograms) provide some qualitative support for the claimed mechanism (that DGCL embeds demographic structure usefully).
Architectural and implementation details (Appendix B, C) are reported with reasonable specificity (hyperparameters, channel/sampling-rate tables, dataset splits), aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: Results are inconsistent and the paper's strongest performance claims are not well supported: on the KISS sleep-staging benchmark, a generic time-series model (MOMENT) outperforms SleepMaMi, and the explanation offered (hardware/sensor distribution shift) is speculative, with no controlled experiment (e.g., training/testing on matched hardware) to substantiate it.

Disease prediction results (Table 3) are mixed rather than clearly superior — SleepMaMi loses to SleepFM-Disease on 3 of 6 outcomes (CVD death, CHD death, Stroke) — yet the text states SleepMaMi 'shows comparable performance,' which somewhat overstates a genuinely mixed result given the paper's framing of outperforming baselines 'across a diverse suite of benchmarks.'

Only one true sleep-specific foundation-model baseline (SleepFM-Disease) is compared against, despite numerous other sleep-staging/foundation approaches being discussed in Related Work (e.g., U-Sleep, SleepTransformer, original SleepFM); the absence of these as baselines weakens the significance claims.

No error bars, confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere (classification/segmentation tables, few-shot curves, disease prediction), making it impossible to assess whether reported gains (often a few points) are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially given single train/test splits.

The ablation table (Table 11) conflates several unrelated axes (architecture components AND the switch from single-dataset to large-scale pretraining) in a single monotonic sequence, making it hard to isolate the individual contribution of each proposed component (shared/private encoder, MAE, CL, scale, DGCL) — a full factorial or at least decoupled ablation would be more convincing.

The claim of ~10 hours end-to-end pretraining on 158K hours of multi-modal PSG data with MoE layers and two dual-stream hierarchical encoders on just 2 GPUs is surprising and insufficiently detailed (e.g., no mention of batch throughput, FLOPs, or epoch counts per encoder relative to data size) to be independently verified; this raises reproducibility concerns.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is unclear: baselines are evaluated with 'the same input unless specific settings are required,' but it is not stated whether baseline models were retrained/fine-tuned from their original pretrained checkpoints under comparable compute/epoch budgets, or whether architecture-specific preprocessing differences (e.g., sampling rate 256Hz for SleepFM) could bias results.

The training schedules used for pretraining (3 epochs micro, 4 epochs macro) and downstream fine-tuning (3 epochs) are very short for models of this scale and complexity (MoE, multiple transformer/Mamba stacks); it's unclear whether models have converged, especially for baselines being retrained under the same short regimes.

Originality claims ('the first foundation model that explicitly encodes both micro- and macro-structural sleep features') may be overstated given related hierarchical approaches (e.g., U-Sleep's multi-scale design, SleepFM-Disease's full-night disease prediction) are not clearly differentiated beyond stating they are mostly micro-structure focused.

The demographic-distance supervisory signal for DGCL (age, BMI, and a fixed sex-mismatch penalty λ_sex=1) is somewhat ad hoc; the specific functional form and penalty weight are not justified theoretically nor ablated for sensitivity, and the assumption that linear demographic distance tracks macro-structural similarity is a strong simplification that isn't validated beyond qualitative figures.

strengths: Novel hierarchical dual-encoder architecture (Micro + Macro) explicitly designed to jointly capture short-term physiological morphology and full-night sleep architecture, addressing a genuine gap in prior sleep foundation models that focus almost exclusively on micro-structure.

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) is a creative and well-motivated idea: using objective, scalable metadata (age, sex, BMI) as a noise-free supervisory signal avoids the inter-scorer variability problems that plague PSG labels, and the paper supports the underlying premise with clear exploratory figures (Fig. 4, 8, 9) showing demographic-dependent macro-structure trends.

Large and diverse pretraining corpus (>20,000 recordings, 158K hours across 7 public datasets) with careful preprocessing and well-documented per-dataset statistics in the appendix, which is valuable for reproducibility.

Broad downstream evaluation suite: sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction (via Cox PH / C-index), few-shot adaptation, and embedding visualization, which together probe both local and global representation quality.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 11, 12) isolate the contribution of private/shared encoders, MAE, CL, large-scale pretraining, and DGCL components, and specific demographic factors, lending some support to the architectural design choices.
Detailed appendix with architecture specs, hyperparameters, and dataset descriptions aids reproducibility even though code availability is not explicitly stated.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is narrow: only one sleep-specific foundation model (SleepFM-Disease) and two general-purpose time-series models are used; the original SleepFM, other self-supervised PSG/EEG methods, or supervised SOTA task-specific models are not included, limiting the strength of 'outperforms existing foundation models' claims.

Results are notably mixed but are framed more positively than warranted: on KISS, SleepMaMi underperforms MOMENT in sleep staging (Table 1), and in disease prediction SleepMaMi loses to SleepFM-Disease on 3 of 6 outcomes (CVD death, CHD death, Stroke) in Table 3, yet is described simply as 'comparable' or the overall narrative emphasizes superiority without fully reconciling these shortfalls.

The explanation for the KISS underperformance (hardware/sensor distribution shift) is only a post-hoc hypothesis; no controlled experiment (e.g., training/testing across matched hardware subsets) is provided to substantiate this claim, weakening the causal interpretation.

No statistical uncertainty is reported anywhere (no confidence intervals, standard deviations across seeds, or significance tests) for any downstream result, including Tables 1-4 and the few-shot curves, making it hard to assess whether observed gains over baselines are robust or within noise.

The reported pretraining time (~10 hours on 2×H100) for 158K hours of multi-modal data with a complex hierarchical architecture (two-stage, MoE, Mamba) is surprisingly fast and raises reproducibility/plausibility questions that are not clarified (e.g., exact number of gradient steps, effective batch/token throughput).

There is no discussion of the ethical implications of conditioning the Macro-Encoder explicitly on demographic attributes (age, sex, BMI). Embedding these factors directly into learned representations risks encoding/leaking protected attributes into downstream clinical predictions and could amplify demographic bias in disease-risk estimation; this is not addressed in the limitations.

Most downstream evaluations rely on linear probing of frozen representations rather than full fine-tuning, which is a reasonable way to assess representation quality but may not reflect the model's practical ceiling performance or how baselines would perform under full fine-tuning, and this distinction/justification is not deeply discussed.

No external, truly held-out clinical site or population is used to rigorously test generalization beyond the KISS distribution-shift anecdote; the few-shot evaluation on ISRUC is useful but still fairly small-scale.

Related work coverage of competing self-supervised PSG/EEG representation learning approaches (e.g., other contrastive or masked modeling works beyond SleepFM) is relatively thin, making it harder to contextualize the novelty of the hybrid MAE+CL micro-encoder design relative to the broader SSL-for-biosignals literature.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap in sleep representation learning by explicitly modeling both micro-structure (second-scale biosignal morphology) and macro-structure (full-night sleep architecture) within a unified hierarchical framework, rather than the epoch-level focus of prior sleep foundation models (SleepFM, OSF, Sleep2Vec, etc.).

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) is a well-motivated and reasonably novel idea: using objective, scalable metadata (age, sex, BMI) as a supervisory signal for macro-structure pretraining sidesteps the well-documented inter-scorer variability and evolving AASM guideline issues that plague label-based sleep staging supervision. The empirical visualization in Figure 4 supporting the demographic-macrostructure link is a nice motivating analysis.

Pretraining corpus is large and diverse (>20,000 PSG recordings, 158K hours, 8+ cohorts across multiple countries/manufacturers), and the paper evaluates on both in-distribution (SHHS1, KISS) and fully held-out external cohorts (CFS, SOF, ISRUC), which is a meaningful test of generalization.

Broad evaluation suite: sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction (via Cox PH/C-index), few-shot adaptation, and an ablation program covering core components, demographic factors, cycle length, Macro-Encoder architecture choice, and alternative pretraining objectives (SimCLR, DINO) — this is a fairly comprehensive empirical treatment for a systems-level contribution.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility (detailed architecture tables, hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing, channel/sampling-rate tables in the appendix) and to fairness/ethics considerations (subgroup analysis for demographic bias in Appendix E, explicit Impact Statement discussion).
weaknesses: The abstract/main text claim that SleepMaMi 'outperforms or matches state-of-the-art foundation models' is accurate only relative to other foundation models; comparisons to fully supervised, task-specialized models (Table 17, 19, appendix) reveal SleepMaMi trailing considerably in several cases (e.g., SDB segmentation Macro-F1 60.6 vs. AIX's 74.6 on SHHS1; sleep staging accuracy gaps of 1–5 points vs. SleePyCo/DistillSleep). This important caveat is relegated to the appendix rather than discussed prominently in the main paper, giving a somewhat inflated impression of the method's absolute standing.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper (pretraining or downstream fine-tuning); all reported numbers appear to be single runs, which weakens confidence in the many close margins observed (e.g., DGCL vs. SimCLR/DINO ablation differs by only ~0.1–0.2 points, Table 16).

Baseline coverage is inconsistent across tasks: disease prediction (Table 3) is compared only against SleepFM-Disease, omitting the time-series and EEG foundation model baselines used elsewhere, which limits the strength of the disease-prediction contribution claim. Similarly, LaBraM is dropped from CFS/SOF sleep-staging and SDB tables without clear justification.

SDB segmentation and staging results occasionally show accuracy decreasing while Macro-F1 increases relative to baselines (e.g., SOF SDB: SleepMaMi accuracy 70.2 vs. UniTS 90.6, though Macro-F1 favors SleepMaMi), suggesting the model may be trading off majority-class performance for minority-class sensitivity; this behavior deserves more direct discussion/analysis (e.g., calibration, precision-recall trade-off) rather than being framed solely as a class-imbalance artifact.

The demographic distance function underlying DGCL (equal weighting of z-scored age and BMI plus a fixed sex penalty) is acknowledged as empirically chosen but not rigorously validated against alternative formulations; the ablation against SimCLR/DINO tests different learning objectives but does not probe sensitivity to the distance metric itself, leaving the core design choice under-justified.

Reproducibility is nominally supported by extensive appendix detail, but the actual code/checkpoint URL is left blank in the submission ('Our source code and checkpoint are available at'), so the promised release cannot be verified at review time.

The technical architecture, while carefully engineered, largely combines existing building blocks (MAE, contrastive learning, MoE, RoPE/SwiGLU/RMSNorm Transformers, bidirectional Mamba) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; the primary originality lies in the systems-level integration and the DGCL objective, which is a reasonable but incremental contribution for a top-tier venue.

Several of the comparator citations (Thapa et al. 2026 Nature Medicine, Huang et al. 2026 Nature Communications, Yuan et al. 2026 ICLR, Shuai et al. 2026 ICML, Lee et al. 2026 ICLR) are dated 2026, which, while plausibly valid as concurrently accepted work, makes independent verification of claimed baseline results difficult for reviewers at this stage.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap in sleep representation learning: jointly modeling second-scale micro-structure and full-night macro-structure within a single foundation model, rather than treating them as separate problems.

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) is a reasonably novel idea that substitutes noisy, inter-scorer-variable sleep stage labels with objective, scalable metadata (age, sex, BMI) as a training signal for the Macro-Encoder; the motivating analysis (Fig. 4, 8, 9) showing demographic-dependent macro-structure patterns is a nice piece of exploratory evidence.

Large and diverse pretraining corpus (>20K PSG recordings, 158K hours across 9 datasets) and evaluation on multiple held-out external datasets (CFS, SOF, ISRUC) provides some evidence of cross-cohort generalization.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (core component ablation, demographic-factor ablation, cycle-length ablation, Macro-Encoder architecture ablation, alternative pretraining-objective ablation) and a dedicated subgroup bias analysis for the DGCL design.

Detailed architectural and training hyperparameter documentation in the appendix (patch sizes, masking schemes, loss weights, optimizer settings), which aids reproducibility of the described pipeline.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the abstract/intro claim SleepMaMi 'outperforms or matches state-of-the-art foundation models,' but it is never empirically compared against the most directly relevant and recently published competitors explicitly discussed in Related Work (Sleep2Vec, OSF, SleepGPT, original SleepFM) — only a disease-prediction variant (SleepFM-Disease) is used as the sleep-FM baseline, which is a significant omission given these are the closest prior works.

Results are inconsistent across tables/metrics in ways that undercut the headline claims: e.g., in Table 2 SleepMaMi has lower raw accuracy than baselines on CFS and SOF SDB segmentation (79.9 vs 85.5, 70.2 vs 90.6), and Table 19 shows a large gap versus a task-specialized SDB model (93.8/74.6 vs 77.3/60.6), weakening the paper's core 'universal model matches specialized models' narrative.

The magnitude of improvement over SleepFM-Disease shrinks dramatically when switching from linear probing (Table 1, often >10-point gaps) to LSTM fine-tuning (Table 17, gaps of ~1 point or less), raising concerns that the large linear-probing gaps may partly reflect suboptimal baseline tuning rather than genuinely superior representations.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported for any experiment (staging, SDB, disease prediction, few-shot, ablations), making it impossible to judge whether reported differences (often 1-2 points) are meaningful or within noise.

Reproducibility concerns: the promised code/checkpoint link is left blank in the manuscript, and the pretraining pipeline (two-stage, large-scale, multi-dataset, custom harmonization of SDB labels via a separate unpublished protocol) is complex enough that independent replication without released artifacts is unlikely.

The DGCL supervisory signal (age, sex, BMI) is a coarse, low-dimensional proxy for 'macro-structure' and the distance function/ weighting scheme (Eq. 5) is hand-designed with an ad hoc sex penalty constant; the ablation in Table 13 shows the gain from using all three demographic factors together (80.7%) is small relative to using BMI alone (80.1%) or age alone (80.6%), suggesting the added complexity may not be strongly justified by the evidence.

Confusion matrices (Appendix F.5) reveal quite poor N1 classification (33-38% accuracy) and substantial class confusion, which is not discussed in the main text despite N1 scoring being clinically important and a common differentiator of model quality.

The ablation Table 12 is somewhat confusingly structured (e.g., row 4 removes the shared encoder but keeps CL, producing a large accuracy drop to 67.7% without clear explanation of why this configuration was chosen over other logical ablations), making it hard to cleanly attribute gains to specific design choices.

Citations to several very recently dated (2026) venues for directly competing methods are used to justify both the related-work framing and omission from experimental comparison, which is a presentation weakness since readers cannot verify these comparisons were infeasible at submission time.

strengths: Large-scale, diverse pretraining corpus (>20,000 PSG recordings, 158K hours across 8+ public datasets) with careful preprocessing and dataset documentation in the appendix, which is a solid empirical foundation.

The core idea of explicitly modeling both micro-structure (second-scale events) and macro-structure (full-night architecture) via a hierarchical dual-encoder is a sensible and underexplored direction relative to existing sleep foundation models that mostly operate on fixed epochs.

Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning is a creative way to obtain an objective, label-free supervisory signal for macro-structure that avoids inter-scorer variability in manual PSG scoring; the motivating visualizations (Fig. 4, 8, 9) support the premise that demographics modulate sleep architecture.

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple downstream tasks (sleep staging, SDB segmentation, disease prediction), held-out cross-cohort generalization (CFS, SOF), few-shot/label-efficiency experiments, and a reasonably thorough ablation suite (component ablations, demographic factor ablations, cycle-length ablations, architecture ablations, alternative macro pretraining strategies).

Transparent reporting of limitations relative to task-specialized models (Tables 17, 19) and an explicit subgroup/bias analysis for the demographic-guided objective (Appendix E), which strengthens trust in the claims rather than overselling them.
Reasonable engineering choices (bi-directional Mamba for efficient long-sequence modeling, patch merging, private-shared encoder design) with memory/efficiency comparisons included.
weaknesses: The paper's abstract/intro claim that SleepMaMi 'outperforms or matches' state-of-the-art models is only partially supported: against task-specialized sleep-staging models and an SDB-specific model, SleepMaMi is clearly and sometimes substantially worse (e.g., AIX: 93.8% vs. 77.3% accuracy and 74.6 vs. 60.6 Macro-F1 on SHHS1 SDB segmentation; SleePyCo/DistillSleep outperform on sleep staging). This caveat is disclosed in the appendix but undersells the gap in the main text framing.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed runs are reported for any main results table, making it difficult to judge whether reported gains over baselines (sometimes only 1-2 points) are robust rather than noise.

The promised code/checkpoint release sentence is incomplete ('Our source code and checkpoint are available at' with no link provided), undermining the reproducibility claim; combined with substantial undocumented hyperparameter/implementation complexity (private-shared transformers, MoE routing, hierarchical patch merging with masking alignment), independent reproduction would be challenging without the actual release.

The demographic distance function in DGCL (linear combination of normalized age/BMI differences plus a fixed sex penalty) is acknowledged as empirically/heuristically designed; no principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond cycle-length and factor-inclusion ablations is given, and the fixed λ_sex penalty choice is not justified or ablated.

Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental/combinatorial: the micro-encoder largely assembles existing techniques (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, MoE, MAE, contrastive learning, patch merging) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; the main novel element is the application of a metadata-driven contrastive objective (DGCL) to macro-structure modeling, which itself resembles existing distance-weighted/soft-target contrastive formulations (e.g., SimPER-style weighting) applied to a new context.

It is unclear from the main text whether baseline foundation models (MOMENT, UniTS, LaBraM, SleepFM-Disease) were given comparable compute/pretraining-data scale or only evaluated via linear probing on public checkpoints; fairness of comparison (e.g., whether baselines could also benefit from similar data scale) is not fully addressed, which weakens claims of SleepMaMi's superiority being attributable to the proposed architecture/objectives rather than data scale alone.

The contribution, while solid for the clinical sleep analysis community, is narrow in scope for a general ML venue like ICML; broader methodological insights that would transfer to other multi-scale time-series domains are not strongly articulated beyond the specific PSG application.
